newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 18.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. For further information on these articles or details of BMC's other international press and broadcast services call Simon McMillan on +44 (0)171 256 5130 or e-mail bmc.co@ft.com
-- SALE OF FIGHTER JETS TO INDONESIA SET TO GO AHEAD

Despite accusations Indonesia had been using previously acquired jets in East Timor, the British government seems likely to allow British Aerospace to complete the sale of 16 Hawk fighter aircraft to the country. Ministers have announced the deal will not be halted due to 'formidable obstacles' involved in revoking the contract. The British arms industry has welcomed the government decision, relieved no damaging foreign policy will be introduced.
-- NATIONWIDE REBELS MAY WIN KEY BALLOT

Indications Nationwide building society is to be converted into a bank were raised on Thursday, as it was revealed there had been an overwhelming show of support for controversial elections to its board. Former royal butler Michael Hardern is leading a team of five rebel Nationwide members seeking election on a pro-conversion ticket, a team that is being opposed by five existing board members committed to mutuality. Complete results of a Nationwide postal ballot will be revealed at its annual meeting on Thursday.
-- BT AND MCI AT ODDS OVER WHEN LOSSES WERE REVEALED

British Telecom and MCI are locked in a debate over when BT was first informed of MCI's financial difficulties. MCI claim BT first heard of its higher-than-expected losses in March 1997 and that the UK telecoms giant received continuous updates into the worsening state of MCI finances. BT labelled the MCI statement 'not true' maintaining it knew nothing of the extent of MCI's problems until late last week, when the US group revealed it could lose up to $800m this year on domestic expansion plans.
-- CLINTON AND CHIRAC JOIN ROW OVER BOEING MERGER

US president Bill Clinton and French president Jacques Chirac have entered the debate into the proposed merger of US aircraft manufacturers Boeing and McDonnell Douglas. Clinton has warned the European Commission if the deal is blocked, his administration will retaliate and Chirac commented that the Commission must maintain its stand against the merger, as it represents 'an attack' on the commercial interests of Europe such as Airbus Industrie.
-- CARD SPENDING RISES TO RECORD 8.2BN STG IN JUNE

The Credit Card Research Group, a payment card industry association, has revealed that consumers in Britain spent a record 8.2m stg in June on their debit and credit cards, a figure that pushes full-year spending towards 100bn stg. The biggest increase came in the use of Switch and Visa Electron cards, which take money directly from a bank account rather than rolling payments into a monthly bill. Total debit card spending reached 3.63bn stg, taking the first-half total to 20.4bn stg.
-- STRONG POUND HITS EXPORTS IN NORTH-WEST

A survey of 530 manufacturers and 544 service companies carried out by the North West Chamber of Commerce has shown the strength of sterling led to a fall in export orders for north-west England in the second quarter. The survey exposes a 'two speed economy' in the region and indicates there is no immediate sign of sterling easing, leading to expectations there will be further pressure on the export market over the short term at least.
-- CHANCELLOR CLARIFIES EMU JOINING CONDITIONS

Chancellor Gordon Brown clarified on Thursday the five conditions the government has provided for Britain's entry into the single currency. Speaking to the Royal Institute of Foreign Affairs, Brown stated UK entry into Emu was likely if it created better conditions for companies to invest in the UK, if it promoted higher growth and more jobs, if it proved capable to cope with economic shocks, if UK and mainland business cycles and economic structures proved to be compatible and if its effect on the UK financial services industry could be specifically assessed.
-- EMI IN 20M STG PUBLISHING DEAL

Popular British recording artist Sting has sold global publishing rights to his songs to EMI for 20m stg, a deal that covers all of his songs from the late 1970s to the present. It was revealed that Sting had been in negotiations with EMI for four months before an agreement was reached, and the deal had been signalled as a highlight of the appeal of music publishing, which is fast becoming the most profitable sector of the music industry.
-- ICI TO RAISE $500M FROM BONDS

Imperial Chemical Industries is seeking to raise 299m stg from the eurobond market in the near future as the first stage of its $4bn fundraising efforts to reduce the cost of its borrowing. ICI has not sought funds from the market since 1993, when its pharmaceuticals business, Zeneca, was demerged in 1993. The new move will substantially increase the availability of ICI debt. Joint lead managers UBS and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell intend the new bond to be a benchmark issue.
-- DISPLAY.IT SUSPENDED AS SOLICITOR RESIGNS

At its own request, Internet software company Display.IT shares were suspended on Thursday, after the resignation of the group's solicitor. Taylor Joynson Garrett withdrew from Display.IT due to the inability of the company secretary, Tom Mackay, to obtain certain information from the company concerning its affairs. Display.IT and its chief executive Peter Levin were in meetings on Thursday and issued no statements concerning the latest development.
